items.name: Saigon wakes up
items.tagline: A walk as the city opens its eyes
items.text: Three hours on foot before the traffic starts: sock-filter coffee at the mouth of an alley, the morning market, the cathedral, the post office and an old apartment block.

image.alt: A barista pours hot water through a cloth filter to make coffee at a District 3 café

stages.text: Meet your guide, grab some water, stretch your legs.
Coffee brewed through a cloth sock, on plastic stools at the alley mouth.

image.alt: A barista pours hot water through a cloth filter to make coffee at a District 3 café

stages.text: Sticky rice, steamed rice rolls, hot banh mi. Eating standing up is fine.

image.alt: A crusty banh mi filled with meat, pickles and green chilli, held in one hand

stages.text: Two buildings over a hundred years old, photographed while the sun is still low.

image.alt: The yellow facade of Saigon Central Post Office under a blue sky, visitors strolling outside

stages.text: Through an alley with a vegetable market and lantern-hung townhouses.

image.alt: A narrow District 3 alley, vegetable sellers on the kerb, townhouses hung with lanterns

stages.text: The end. Want to keep going? Your guide will point the way.

bring: Covered shoulders if you want to go inside the cathedral

items.name: Cho Lon alleys
items.tagline: By cyclo through the Chinese quarter
items.text: A van to District 5, then cyclos through the herbal medicine street and lantern street, stopping at Binh Tay Market and Thien Hau Temple.

image.alt: The clock tower and curved tiled roofs of Binh Tay Market in Cho Lon under a cloudy sky

stages.text: A 16-seat van picks you up at the meeting point, 30 minutes to Cho Lon.
A century-old wholesale market, busiest at this hour, goods stacked to the ceiling.

image.alt: The clock tower and curved tiled roofs of Binh Tay Market in Cho Lon under a cloudy sky

stages.text: Onto the cyclos, one per person, rolling slowly through the trade streets.

image.alt: A cyclo driver pedalling down a Saigon street

stages.text: Giant incense coils hanging from the ceiling, smoke drifting in the sunlight.

image.alt: Rows of incense burners with red sticks smoking inside Thien Hau Temple, Cho Lon

stages.text: Dumplings, siu mai and hot tea at a third-generation shop.
The van drops you at the meeting point.

bring: Small cash if you want to buy things

items.name: Thanh Da by bike
items.tagline: Village lanes in the middle of the city
items.text: A peninsula wrapped by the Saigon River, 6 km from the centre yet still full of village lanes, vegetable gardens and a river ferry.

image.alt: A street vendor's bicycle loaded with pomelos and bananas on a Saigon pavement

stages.text: Adjust the saddle, put on a helmet, a test lap.
Water palms, old stilt houses, almost no cars.

image.alt: A street vendor's bicycle loaded with pomelos and bananas on a Saigon pavement

stages.text: Wheel your bike onto the boat, five minutes to the other bank.

image.alt: The bow of a green wooden boat gliding on the Saigon River, downtown towers in the distance

stages.text: Coconut water while the gardener tells how the family kept its land.
Stop on the dyke and watch the sun go down behind the towers.

image.alt: The Saigon River curving around the Binh Thanh peninsula at sunset

stages.text: The end.

items.name: Saigon River at dusk
items.tagline: Small boat, small canals, the sun going down
items.text: Leave Bach Dang pier in an eight-seat wooden boat, slip into a small canal, reach the main river right at sunset and come back as the city lights up.

image.alt: The Saigon River curving around the Binh Thanh peninsula at sunset

stages.text: Board the boat, life jackets, cold water.
The boat glides slowly under low bridges.

image.alt: The bow of a green wooden boat gliding on the Saigon River, downtown towers in the distance

stages.text: Sunset over Thu Thiem, the water turns orange.

image.alt: The Saigon River curving around the Binh Thanh peninsula at sunset

stages.text: Fresh spring rolls, sweet soup, sugarcane juice.
The towers switch on their lights one by one.

image.alt: The downtown Saigon skyline lit up at night, reflected in the river

items.name: Saigon after dark
items.tagline: On the back of a motorbike, seven dishes
items.text: One driver per guest, four districts, seven dishes at the places Saigon locals eat, then the city seen from above.

image.alt: A Saigon intersection at night seen from above, motorbikes and cars turned into bright light trails

stages.text: Your driver hands you a helmet, a raincoat waits under the seat.
Chilli clams, scallops grilled with scallion oil.

image.alt: A plate of chilli-fried clams with fresh herbs at a seafood stall

stages.text: Glutinous rice balls and jelly drinks at a forty-year-old shop.
Grilled rice paper, on plastic stools right by the kerb.

image.alt: A vendor standing by a steaming pot of broth at a late-night alley stall

stages.text: A hot crusty loaf with homemade pâté.

image.alt: A crusty banh mi filled with meat, pickles and green chilli, held in one hand

stages.text: Watch the traffic below turn into trails of light.

image.alt: The downtown Saigon skyline lit up at night, reflected in the river

stages.text: Your driver takes you to the door.

items.name: Early Cu Chi
items.tagline: At the tunnels before the crowds
items.text: Leave the city at 6 to reach the tunnels while the forest is still cool and before the big tour buses arrive.

image.alt: A small hidden tunnel entrance among dry leaves at the foot of a tree, Cu Chi Tunnels

stages.text: A 16-seat van, a light breakfast on board.
Through the gate just as the site opens.

image.alt: A dirt path leading to a thatched hut in the bamboo forest at the Cu Chi Tunnels site

stages.text: Camouflaged hatches, the smokeless Hoang Cam kitchen, the command bunker.
A widened section of tunnel; if you are not keen, take the short stretch.

image.alt: A small hidden tunnel entrance among dry leaves at the foot of a tree, Cu Chi Tunnels

stages.text: What people living in the tunnels used to eat.
Back in District 1 around 12:30.

items.name: Can Gio mangroves
items.tagline: Van, ferry, speedboat, then a walk in the mangroves
items.text: One day, four ways to travel: a van to the pier, a ferry across the river, a speedboat into the mangroves, then a walk on wooden boardwalks through the wetland forest.

image.alt: Dark green Can Gio mangrove forest stretching along the riverbank

stages.text: A 16-seat van to the ferry pier.
Stand among hundreds of motorbikes crossing the river, a salty breeze.

image.alt: A ferry carrying people and motorbikes across the river, a line of palms on the far bank

stages.text: The speedboat slips into narrow creeks, mangrove roots on both sides.

image.alt: A speedboat cutting through the river, dark green trees on the bank behind

stages.text: Walk the wooden boardwalks, meet the monkeys, storks and herons.

image.alt: Dark green Can Gio mangrove forest stretching along the riverbank

stages.text: Braised fish, prawns and bitter greens at a seaside restaurant.
A stop at the market for anyone who wants dried seafood to take home.

image.alt: A fish seller among basins of fresh fish at a country market

stages.text: Back in District 1 around 17:00.

bring: No snacks in hand (the monkeys grab them)

items.text: The driver rode as slowly as a stroll and stopped right where I wanted photos. Seven dishes and I still wanted an eighth.
My first cyclo ride, and the driver told stories about Cho Lon the whole way. My daughter remembers every street name.
A ferry, then a speedboat, then a walk in the forest. One day that felt like three different trips.
I had half a day free between two meetings and booked the early tour. Back at the hotel in time to shower and go to work.
The canal got so narrow we had to duck under the bridges. Sunset on the big river was better than I imagined.
I never thought there were village lanes to cycle right in the city. The coconut water in the garden was so sweet.

items.question: How far ahead should I book?
items.answer: For group tours, 2 hours ahead is fine if seats are left. For private tours, book 2 days ahead so SighGone can arrange vehicles and people.

items.question: Do I need to pay in advance?
items.answer: No. Send a hold message, SighGone calls to confirm, then pay in cash or by bank transfer when you meet your guide.

items.question: Can I come on my own?
items.answer: Yes, plenty of people travel solo. You join a group of up to 8; on the motorbike tour everyone has their own driver.

items.question: Can I eat vegetarian?
items.answer: Yes. Add a note when you book and the places switch to vegetarian dishes for you, same price.

items.question: Which tours are good for kids?
items.answer: Daytime tours take kids of any age, under 6 free. The evening motorbike tour takes kids from 6, riding with a parent.

items.question: What if it rains?
items.answer: Light rain, we still go, raincoats provided. Heavy rain or high tide, SighGone calls 3 hours ahead to reschedule, free of charge.

items.question: Do I lose money if I cancel?
items.answer: Cancel more than 24 hours ahead: full refund. Within 24 hours: half refund. No-show without notice: no refund.

items.question: Where do you pick me up?
items.answer: The meeting point at the Opera House is free. Hotel pickup in District 1 or 3 adds 50,000 VND per group.

items.question: Do you drop me back at my hotel?
items.answer: Motorbike tours and tours with the 16-seat van drop you at the door. Walking and cycling tours end in the centre; your guide can call you a ride.

sections.title: Say Sài Gòn fast and it sounds like Sigh Gone
sections.lead: The two falling tone marks are two sighs; one trip and they're gone.

sections.title: Say it fast: Saigon
story: Saigon people sigh a lot: traffic, sun, afternoon rain, deadlines. The SighGone team grew up here and knows the corners where people forget to sigh.
SighGone started in 2019 with one motorbike and one late-night food tour. Now there are 27 guides, six ways to get around, and one rule: no group bigger than 8.

quote.text: Say "Sài Gòn" fast and it comes out as "Sigh Gone": the sigh flies away.

items.question: How far ahead should I book?
items.answer: For shared tours, 2 hours ahead is fine if there are seats. For private tours, book 2 days ahead so SighGone can arrange vehicles and people.

items.question: Do I pay in advance?
items.answer: No. Send a hold message, SighGone calls to confirm, then pay cash or by transfer when you meet your guide.

items.question: Can I go alone?
items.answer: Yes, plenty of people do. You join a group of up to 8, and on motorbike tours everyone has their own driver.

items.question: Can I eat vegetarian?
items.answer: Yes. Add a note when you hold your seat and the eateries switch to vegetarian dishes, same price.

items.question: Which tours suit children?
items.answer: Daytime tours take children of any age, free under 6. Night motorbike tours take children from 6, riding with a parent.

items.question: What if it rains?
items.answer: Light rain, we still go, with raincoats. Heavy rain or high tide, SighGone calls 3 hours ahead to reschedule at no cost.

items.question: Do I lose money if I cancel?
items.answer: Cancel more than 24 hours ahead: full refund. Within 24 hours: half refund. No-show without notice: no refund.

items.question: Where do you pick me up?
items.answer: The meeting point at the Saigon Opera House is free. Hotel pick-up in District 1 or 3 is 50,000 VND extra per group.

items.question: Do you drop me back at my hotel?
items.answer: Motorbike tours and tours with a 16-seat van drop you at your door. Walking and cycling tours end in the centre, and your guide can call a ride if needed.
